title: BFS on Implicit State Graphs
subject: Graph Algorithms
statement: BFS works when vertices are states generated on the fly rather than stored explicitly, provided neighbours can be enumerated and duplicates detected.
short: Build the graph as you explore it.
long: Build the graph as you explore it. A visited set keyed by canonical state prevents revisits in graphs with converging transitions.
proof: The queue discipline depends only on neighbour generation, not on an explicit adjacency matrix.
consequence: This is the standard model for solving puzzles, protocol reachability and game states.

title: Minimum Spanning Tree Cut Property
subject: Graph Algorithms
statement: For any cut, a minimum-weight edge crossing it belongs to every minimum spanning tree if its weight is strictly smaller than all other crossing edges.
short: The cheapest bridge across a divide is safe to include.
long: The cheapest bridge across a divide is safe to include. Ties can make some but not all minimum crossing edges part of an MST.
proof: If an MST omits e, adding e creates a cycle crossing the cut; removing a heavier crossing edge yields a lighter tree.
consequence: The cut property justifies Kruskal's and Prim's greedy choices.

title: Minimum Spanning Tree Cycle Property
subject: Graph Algorithms
statement: The heaviest edge on any cycle cannot belong to a minimum spanning tree if its weight is strictly larger than every other edge on that cycle.
short: An over-heavy cycle edge is never needed.
long: An over-heavy cycle edge is never needed. With equal weights the statement requires the unique-heaviest condition.
proof: If an MST contained e, removing e splits the tree; some other cycle edge reconnects the parts with smaller weight.
consequence: The cycle property justifies reverse-delete algorithms.

title: Kruskal's Algorithm with Union-Find
subject: Graph Algorithms
statement: Sorting edges by weight and adding each edge that connects different components builds a minimum spanning tree in O(E log E) time.
short: Greedily add the cheapest edge that does not form a cycle.
long: Greedily add the cheapest edge that does not form a cycle. Union-find tests component membership; ties in weight are handled arbitrarily.
proof: When an edge is added it is the cheapest crossing the cut between its component and the rest, so the cut property applies.
consequence: Kruskal is simple and efficient for sparse graphs.

title: Prim's Algorithm with a Priority Queue
subject: Graph Algorithms
statement: Growing a single tree by repeatedly adding the cheapest edge to an outside vertex yields an MST in O(E log V) with a binary heap.
short: Expand the frontier one vertex at a time.
long: Expand the frontier one vertex at a time. With a Fibonacci heap the amortised bound is O(E + V log V).
proof: The chosen edge is cheapest across the cut separating the current tree from unvisited vertices, so the cut property applies.
consequence: Prim is efficient on dense graphs and natural when starting from a given vertex.

title: Prim with Fibonacci Heap Bound
subject: Graph Algorithms
statement: Using a Fibonacci heap, Prim's algorithm runs in O(E + V log V) amortised time.
short: Cheap decrease-key operations accelerate dense MST construction.
long: Cheap decrease-key operations accelerate dense MST construction. Each edge triggers at most one decrease-key, which is O(1) amortised in a Fibonacci heap.
proof: There are O(E) heap updates and O(V) extract-mins costing O(log V) amortised.
consequence: This matches the best known bounds for dense-graph MST.

title: Boruvka's Parallel MST Algorithm
subject: Graph Algorithms
statement: Boruvka repeatedly adds the cheapest outgoing edge of every component, reducing the number of components by at least half in each phase.
short: Every component simultaneously picks its cheapest exit.
long: Every component simultaneously picks its cheapest exit. The phase structure makes it attractive in parallel and distributed settings.
proof: At least half of the components merge in each round because each chosen edge merges two components.
consequence: It is one of the oldest MST algorithms and still used in parallel implementations.

title: Reverse-Delete MST Algorithm
subject: Graph Algorithms
statement: Sorting edges from most to least expensive and deleting an edge whenever the graph stays connected leaves a minimum spanning tree.
short: Discard the most expensive edge that is not essential.
long: Discard the most expensive edge that is not essential. A straightforward connectivity test per edge makes it slower than Kruskal or Prim.
proof: A deleted edge is the heaviest on some cycle, so it cannot be in an MST by the cycle property.
consequence: It is a clean illustration of the duality between cut and cycle properties.

title: Distinct Edge Weights Imply Unique MST
subject: Graph Algorithms
statement: If all edge weights in a connected graph are distinct, the minimum spanning tree is unique.
short: No tie means every greedy choice is forced.
long: No tie means every greedy choice is forced. With equal weights multiple MSTs can coexist, but Kruskal still produces one valid MST.
proof: If two MSTs differed, take the lightest edge where they differ; the cut property forces it into both, a contradiction.
consequence: Uniqueness simplifies sensitivity analysis and algorithm correctness arguments.

title: Every MST Is a Minimum Bottleneck Tree
subject: Graph Algorithms
statement: Every minimum spanning tree is also a minimum bottleneck spanning tree, minimising the largest edge weight, though the converse need not hold.
short: Minimising total weight also minimises the worst edge.
long: Minimising total weight also minimises the worst edge. A bottleneck-optimal tree can still have larger total weight than an MST.
proof: If a tree had a smaller maximum edge, the MST edge introducing that bottleneck would violate the cut property.
consequence: MST algorithms can be reused for bottleneck connectivity problems.

title: MST Algorithm Choice by Graph Density
subject: Graph Algorithms
statement: Kruskal is O(E log E) and often best for sparse graphs, while Prim with a simple array is O(V^2) and better for dense graphs.
short: Edge sorting versus vertex scanning.
long: Edge sorting versus vertex scanning. Fibonacci-heap Prim improves dense cases to O(E + V log V).
proof: Kruskal's cost is dominated by sorting E edges; array-based Prim scans all V vertices for each of V additions.
consequence: Graph representation and density determine the best MST implementation.

title: MST Is Not a Shortest-Path Tree
subject: Graph Algorithms
statement: An MST rooted at s need not give shortest paths from s; with edges s-a of weight 1, a-b of weight 1 and s-b of weight 1.5, the MST uses s-a and a-b, so its path to b costs 2 while the shortest path costs 1.5.
short: Minimising total tree weight is a different objective.
long: Minimising total tree weight is a different objective. Conversely, a shortest-path tree need not be a minimum spanning tree.
proof: MST minimises sum of edges; shortest-path tree minimises root distances, and no inclusion relation holds in general.
consequence: Use Dijkstra for distances and MST algorithms for network-wide cost minimisation.

title: Odd Cycles Characterise Bipartite Graphs
subject: Graph Algorithms
statement: An undirected graph is bipartite if and only if it contains no cycle of odd length.
short: Two-colouring fails exactly when an odd cycle forces a conflict.
long: Two-colouring fails exactly when an odd cycle forces a conflict. BFS or DFS colouring detects such a conflict in O(V+E) time.
proof: Colouring by parity of distance from a source is consistent unless an edge joins same-parity vertices, which creates an odd cycle.
consequence: Bipartiteness tests are linear and underpin bipartite matching applications.

title: Bipartite Matching Problem
subject: Graph Algorithms
statement: A matching in a bipartite graph is a set of edges with no shared endpoints; maximum matching maximises their number.
short: Pair up left and right vertices without conflicts.
long: Pair up left and right vertices without conflicts. It models assignment of jobs to workers, students to projects and many other pairing tasks.
proof: The degree constraint encodes that each vertex can be used at most once.
consequence: It is one of the most tractable and widely used combinatorial optimisation problems.

title: Augmenting Paths for Bipartite Matching
subject: Graph Algorithms
statement: Repeatedly finding an augmenting path—an unmatched-starting, unmatched-ending alternating path—increases matching size by one until none exists.
short: Flip a path to add one more pair.
long: Flip a path to add one more pair. A BFS-based search for augmenting paths gives the O(VE) Hopcroft–Karp predecessor algorithm.
proof: Berge's lemma says a matching is maximum iff it admits no augmenting path.
consequence: It provides a simple polynomial algorithm for bipartite matching.

title: Hopcroft–Karp Complexity
subject: Graph Algorithms
statement: Hopcroft–Karp finds a maximum bipartite matching in O(E sqrt(V)) time by finding maximal sets of shortest augmenting paths in each phase.
short: Batch augmentations shorten the number of phases.
long: Batch augmentations shorten the number of phases. Each phase uses DFS layered searches and augments along many vertex-disjoint paths at once.
proof: After sqrt(V) phases, augmenting path lengths have grown enough that at most sqrt(V) further phases remain, with O(E) work each.
consequence: It is the standard efficient algorithm for large bipartite matchings.

title: König's Matching–Vertex Cover Theorem
subject: Graph Algorithms
statement: In a bipartite graph, the size of a maximum matching equals the size of a minimum vertex cover.
short: Bipartite duality makes two different problems equal.
long: Bipartite duality makes two different problems equal. This equality fails in general graphs, where vertex cover is NP-hard.
proof: Given a maximum matching, the set of vertices reachable by alternating paths from unmatched left vertices yields a vertex cover of the same size.
consequence: It gives a polynomial algorithm for minimum vertex cover in bipartite graphs and implies integrality of the LP relaxation.

title: Hungarian Algorithm for Assignment
subject: Graph Algorithms
statement: The Hungarian algorithm solves the n by n minimum-cost perfect assignment problem in O(n^3) time using primal-dual label updates.
short: Dual potentials guide augmentations to an optimal assignment.
long: Dual potentials guide augmentations to an optimal assignment. It is equivalent to shortest augmenting paths in a bipartite matching with reduced costs.
proof: Maintaining feasible dual labels and complementary slackness for the current matching yields optimality when all vertices are matched.
consequence: It underlies optimal assignment in operations research and tracking systems.

title: Gale–Shapley Stable Marriage
subject: Graph Algorithms
statement: Deferred acceptance produces a stable matching in O(n^2) time, with all proposers receiving their best stable partners.
short: Proposals plus rejections converge to a stable pairing.
long: Proposals plus rejections converge to a stable pairing. The version where men propose is men-optimal and women-pessimal among stable matchings.
proof: Rejections only move down preference lists, and termination with no unmatched proposer and no blocking pair follows.
consequence: It is used in school choice, medical residency matching and stable roommate variants.

title: Greedy Fails for General Graph Matching
subject: Graph Algorithms
statement: Choosing the shortest or heaviest edge greedily can yield a non-maximum matching in a general graph.
short: Local pairing decisions can block better global pairings.
long: Local pairing decisions can block better global pairings. In a path of four vertices with centre edge heavy, taking the centre prevents matching both ends.
proof: On vertices a-b-c-d with edges ab, bc, cd, choosing bc leaves only one more edge possible, total 1; choosing ab and cd gives 2.
consequence: General maximum matching requires augmenting-path algorithms such as Edmonds' blossom algorithm.

title: Flow Networks and s-t Cuts
subject: Graph Algorithms
statement: A flow network is a directed graph with capacities, and an s-t cut partitions vertices with s on one side and t on the other; the cut capacity is the sum of outgoing edge capacities.
short: Cuts are bottlenecks separating source from sink.
long: Cuts are bottlenecks separating source from sink. A feasible flow satisfies capacity constraints and conservation at all vertices except s and t.
proof: Every s-t path crosses every cut, so cut capacity bounds the total achievable flow.
consequence: Flows and cuts are dual objects underlying network optimisation.

title: Max-Flow Min-Cut Theorem
subject: Graph Algorithms
statement: In any flow network, the value of a maximum flow equals the capacity of a minimum s-t cut.
short: The best flow is exactly limited by the tightest bottleneck.
long: The best flow is exactly limited by the tightest bottleneck. The residual graph at maximum flow identifies the minimum cut as vertices reachable from s.
proof: Flow across any cut equals flow value, giving weak duality; at maximum flow no augmenting path remains, so reachable set forms a cut whose capacity equals the flow.
consequence: It justifies flow-based algorithms and gives constructive minimum cuts.

title: Ford–Fulkerson Method and Integrality
subject: Graph Algorithms
statement: Repeatedly augmenting along residual paths terminates with a maximum flow for integer capacities, using at most O(E |f*|) augmentations.
short: Integral capacities keep every augmentation progress.
long: Integral capacities keep every augmentation progress. With irrational capacities the method need not terminate or converge to the maximum.
proof: Each augmentation increases flow value by at least one unit when capacities are integers, and the value is bounded by the minimum cut.
consequence: Integrality explains why matching and flow yield integer solutions in combinatorial problems.

title: Edmonds–Karp Polynomial Bound
subject: Graph Algorithms
statement: Choosing shortest augmenting paths by BFS in Ford–Fulkerson gives O(VE^2) time.
short: Shortest paths limit how often an edge can become critical.
long: Shortest paths limit how often an edge can become critical. It was the first strongly polynomial max-flow algorithm.
proof: The distance from s to any vertex in the residual graph never decreases, and a given edge can be saturated at most O(V) times, giving O(VE) augmentations of cost O(E).
consequence: It guarantees polynomial time independent of capacity magnitudes.

title: Dinic's Blocking Flow Algorithm
subject: Graph Algorithms
statement: Dinic builds level graphs and pushes blocking flows, running in O(V^2 E) in general and O(E sqrt(E)) on unit networks.
short: Layered networks make augmentations efficient.
long: Layered networks make augmentations efficient. Current-arc pointers avoid rescanning saturated edges within a phase.
proof: Each phase increases the level of the bottleneck structure, giving at most V phases, and a blocking flow is found in O(VE) via DFS with current arcs.
consequence: It is fast in practice and the basis of many modern max-flow implementations.
